explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul writes, "Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities…" (Romans 13:1). Everyone. He doesn't draw a little circle around the Roman believers and leave the rest out. That one word is wider than my whole bakery.

Right, friend. Paul writes, "Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities…" (Romans 13:1). Everyone is a big word. He doesn't stop at the believers in Rome. I like a word that doesn't leave anybody guessing.

explanations.answer: There is no authority except from God
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul gives his reason right away: "…for there is no authority except that which is from God." Then he adds, "The authorities that exist have been appointed by God." He says why, and he says it plain.

explanations.answer: Rulers always know what is best
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but Paul never says that. Nothing in these verses claims rulers always know best. His reason is, "…there is no authority except that which is from God." It's about where authority comes from, not how smart the person holding it is.

explanations.answer: The law of Moses commands it
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, but Paul doesn't mention the law of Moses in these verses. He gives one reason: "…there is no authority except that which is from God." The Moses idea is a nice thought, but it's not on this page.

That's the word, friend. Paul says whoever resists authority is opposing what God has set in place, "…and those who do so will bring judgment on themselves." Notice who does the bringing. It's the one who resists. That's a lot like grabbing a hot pan with no mitt.

Close in feeling, but not the word Paul uses. He says those who resist "…will bring judgment on themselves." He doesn't mention sickness anywhere in these verses. Keep your eyes on the text and you'll be fine.
Not this one, friend. Paul doesn't say a word about poverty here. He says those who resist authority "…will bring judgment on themselves." Judgment is the word that fits the blank.
Careful, friend, it's the other way around. Paul says, "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad." So good conduct has nothing to fear. It's the bad conduct that should get nervous.
Right. Paul says, "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad." The terror is aimed at bad conduct, not good. Good conduct can relax a little.

You got it, baker. Paul asks, "Do you want to be unafraid of the one in authority?" Then he answers, "Then do what is right, and you will have his approval." He asks the question and gives the answer in the same breath. I wish my recipes were that short.

Not this time, friend. Paul asks, "Do you want to be unafraid of the one in authority?" His answer comes right after: "Then do what is right, and you will have his approval." So the card is true, just the way he said it.
That's it, friend. Paul says, "For he is God's servant for your good." Your good. Not his own, and not somebody far away. It's right there in the verse.
Not quite, friend. Paul says the one in authority is "God's servant for your good." The good in that sentence is yours. He doesn't say it's the ruler's own.
I see the thinking, but Paul doesn't mention the emperor in these verses. He says the one in authority "is God's servant for your good." The good he names is yours, friend.
Right, friend. Paul says the one in authority "does not carry the sword in vain." A sword is not for decoration. That's a serious tool, and Paul wants the point to land.
A scroll sounds official, I'll give you that. But Paul's word is sword: "…he does not carry the sword in vain." The scroll isn't in this verse. The sword is.
Not the key, friend. I know a little about keys, since one never found its door in my old drawer. But Paul says, "…he does not carry the sword in vain." Sword is the word that fills the blank.

Yes, friend. Paul writes, "Therefore it is necessary to submit to authority, not only to avoid punishment, but also as a matter of conscience." So there are two reasons. One is about getting caught, and the other is about your own heart.
Not pride, friend. Paul says it's necessary to submit "not only to avoid punishment, but also as a matter of conscience." Conscience is the second reason. Pride never makes the list.

Good try, but custom isn't in the verse. Paul says to submit "not only to avoid punishment, but also as a matter of conscience." Conscience is the other reason. He doesn't say it's just how things are done.

That's it, friend. Paul says, "This is also why you pay taxes." He follows it with a reason: "For the authorities are God's servants, who devote themselves to their work." Nobody loves the bill, but the verse is clear.
Not tithes, friend. Paul writes, "This is also why you pay taxes." He doesn't say a thing about tithes in these verses. Taxes is the word.
Close, since money is involved, but wages aren't the word here. Paul says, "This is also why you pay taxes." The one paying in this verse is you, and the thing you pay is taxes.

Careful, friend. Taxes and revenue are only the first two things on Paul's list. He goes on: "…respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due" (Romans 13:7). So the list has four things, and the card said only two.

Right. Paul starts with "Pay everyone what you owe him," and then lists four things. Taxes and revenue come first, then "…respect to whom respect is due, honor to whom honor is due." That's a bigger list than the card let on.
